newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Hurt Thai baht seen heading south near-term.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hurt Thai baht seen heading south near-term.

text.p: The Thai baht is expected to continue sliding after hitting another record low on Thursday as investors wait for the government to find the right cure for Thailand's economic crisis, analysts and economists said.
Most of them told Reuters they saw the baht hanging in a tight 31.00-33.00 per dollar range between Thursday and Monday, although some saw it possibly weakening to as far as 35.00.

The baht dove to an historic low of 32.70 on Thursday as investors unloaded the beleaguered currency in favour of the much sought US dollar. Its tumble also rattled other regional currencies, which have been in the doldrums this week.
After reported central bank intervention, the baht steadied later on Thursday to just below the 32 baht level.

"The current level of the baht is not reasonable...but unfortunately, it will remain bearish near-term until there is any good news to lift the gloom," said Irene Cheung, vice president at Merrill Lynch.
"All that the market needs now is a credible package to solve the financial problems," she said.

Thailand is suffering its worst economic slump in more than a decade with 1997 growth set to slow to about four percent from 6.4 percent in 1996. Private economists see the growth level well below the officially touted four percent.
The Thai unit has lost more than 20 percent of its value since July 2 when the government announced a managed float to free the currency from a tightly controlled foreign exchange regime.
Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said on Thursday he expected the currency to stabilise after he unveiled a major economic package within two weeks.
He said the package would help stabilise baht volatility and bring down Thai interest rates, currently among the highest in the region.
"Tackling these problems takes time...but the overall economic picture is not that bad," Thanong said, adding that it was normal for a newly floated currency to fluctuate.
Dealers said the baht slid into a tailspin in a thin market on Thursday as importers and corporate investors sold the currency for U.S. dollars.
They said corporates may have been seeking dollars to repay foreign debt as some creditors stopped rolling over loans.

Also weighing on baht sentiment were troubles in the ailing financial sector. Banks and finance firms, heavily over-exposed to the depressed property sector, are in the process of releasing their non-performing loans data.
Rumours, later denied by the Bank of Thailand, that the authorities would soon remove the two-tier baht market was another factor making players nervous, analysts said.
The two-tier market -- one onshore and one offshore -- was imposed in May by the central bank to cut baht supplies from local sources to speculators who attacked the currency then.

"Investors are very bearish about the baht. There are numerous factors that have shaken confidence," said Jimmy Koh, an economist at Singapore-based research house I.D.E.A. "Everything seems to be happening at the wrong time."
Adding to the jitters were poor earnings results reported this week by several financial institutions and the first $80 million bond default by a Thai corporate, Somprasong Land Plc.
The default heightened a sense of nervousness among creditors at a time when Thailand needed liquidity most, analysts said.
News reports that the opposition was planning to launch a no confidence motion also sent negative signals to the market, although no-confidence debates occur regularly in Thailand.

Other analysts said accepting an International Monetary Fund (IMF) aid package should be a viable option to help Thailand get itself back on track again. The government has said it has no plans to seek such a package.
"What is crucial now is the endorsement from a credible agency like the IMF, otherwise creditors are not likely to pour money in," said an economist with major European investment bank.

"I don't think the package will be as comprehensive as that for Mexico. But if Thailand insists on not taking an IMF package, it will have to come up with concrete and credible solutions to show investors," he said.
